draft.title: Combining techniques
card: No single technique gives a whole structure. Each one answers a different question about an unknown organic compound, so chemists use them together.
Mass spectrometry gives the mass of the molecular ion, which is the molar mass. Infrared spectroscopy shows which functional groups are present, such as O-H or C=O.
Carbon-13 NMR shows how many different carbon environments there are. Proton NMR shows the hydrogen environments and, by splitting, how many neighbouring hydrogens each one has.
A common method is to find the molar mass, list the functional groups, then fit the NMR data to a structure. A proposed structure must match every set of data.
draft.remember: Each technique answers a different question. The right structure must fit all of the data.

a.q: An unknown compound has a molecular ion at m/z 74 and an infrared peak for C=O. What does each result tell you?
opts: Molar mass is 74 and a C=O bond is present
Molar mass is 74 and there are 74 carbon environments
Molar mass is 74 and C=O has two hydrogen neighbours
Molar mass is unknown but a C=O bond is present
a.why: The molecular ion peak gives the molar mass, and the infrared peak shows a C=O bond. The number of carbon environments needs carbon-13 NMR, and hydrogen neighbours need proton NMR, so those options are wrong.
a.clue: Which technique gives mass, and which gives bonds?

b.q: Priya has an unknown compound. Its mass spectrum and infrared spectrum suggest a carboxylic acid with molar mass 88. Which extra data would best help her decide between possible structures with that formula?
opts: Proton NMR splitting patterns showing hydrogen neighbours
A second infrared spectrum showing the same O-H peak
The molecular ion mass again from a repeat run
A calibration curve showing its concentration
b.why: Isomers share the same molar mass and can have the same functional groups. Proton NMR splitting shows how the hydrogens are arranged, so it separates them. Repeating the mass or infrared data adds nothing new.
b.clue: Which technique shows how the atoms are arranged, not just what is present?

a.best: Molar mass is 74 and a C=O bond is present

b.best: Proton NMR splitting patterns showing hydrogen neighbours

problems.detail: The question says 'possible structures with that formula', but no molecular formula is given, only a molar mass (88) and a functional group. Students must infer C4H8O2 themselves. Wording such as 'possible structures that fit these data' would be clearer.
